explanations.haitian-revolution-1791-1804--the-cuban-: The cited account is direct: after the end of slavery in Saint-Domingue at the turn of the nineteenth century, with the Haitian Revolution, Cuba became the most substantial sugar plantation colony in the Caribbean, outperforming the British islands. The richest producer in the world stopped producing and the market went to the island next to it. The revolution’s second effect on Cuba runs the other way and is in the same sources: the white upper class was so afraid of following Haiti that it supported Spanish rule intensely, which is part of why Cuba was still a slave colony of Spain when its neighbours had been republics for two generations.
explanations.the-british-industrial-revolution--slave: The other half of the Williams argument, and the one his critics attacked hardest: that it was the rise of industrial capitalism in Britain that destroyed the slave trade, the West Indian interest having become an obstacle to a manufacturing economy rather than its engine. The Act of 1807 is where that claim is tested, and the cited account of Capitalism and Slavery says Williams wrote it against a historiography that used the abolition acts as a moral pivot. The atlas records the claim as disputed because the dissent is at least as well argued as the thesis.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--cuban-revolution--: The cited account of the revolution names five socioeconomic problems that marked the decade before it, and three of them are this record’s: excessive dependence on sugar cultivation and exports, reliance on the United States for investment and trade, and a low rate of growth. The sugar sector was subject to American quotas and to world prices, it was seasonal and so dragged trade and transport with it, and Cuban capital went into real estate and financial investments in the United States rather than into industry at home. A hundred and sixty-eight years separate the two records and the type is the weak one: the monoculture is what the revolution happened inside, not what made it.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--cuban-war-of-indep: Abolition in 1886 broke the arrangement that had held Cuba to Spain. The freedmen went into the countryside and the towns; the economy could not carry the speed of the reform; wealthy Cubans lost property and fell into the middle class; the mills consolidated into the hands of companies and the largest owners, increasingly American ones. By 1894 ninety per cent of Cuban exports went to the United States and Cuba’s exports to Spain were a twelfth of that. A colony whose commerce had stopped running through its metropole, with a dispossessed creole class in it, is the one that rose in 1895.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--platt-amendment-19: What the settlement of 1901 was written around is named in the sources on both sides of it. Theodore Roosevelt, arguing for the war: "Our own direct interests were great, because of the Cuban tobacco and sugar, and especially because of Cuba’s relation to the projected Isthmian Canal." Some historians read even the Teller Amendment’s ban on annexation as protection for American sugar-beet growers rather than for Cuban independence. And after Cuba accepted the Amendment the United States ratified a tariff giving Cuban sugar preference in the American market and protecting selected American goods in the Cuban one. The type is the weak one because the Amendment’s seven conditions are about troops, treaties and naval stations rather than about cane; the boom is the thing that made Cuba worth writing them about.
explanations.the-cuban-sugar-boom--spanish-american-w: The weakest type, and the sources are the reason it is not a stronger one. American money had been buying into the devalued Cuban sugar market since the Ten Years’ War, and by 1894 the United States held the economic power over Cuba while Spain held the political authority — that is the asymmetry the war resolved. But the sugar investors did not want the war. The cited account has them looking to Spain to restore order, and the shipping firms pressing Washington to end the revolt: stability, not war, was what both wanted. So this edge does not say the sugar interest procured the intervention. It says the intervention happened in a country the United States already owned the economy of, and that this is why intervening was thinkable.
explanations.transfer-of-the-colonial-capital-to-rio-: The court did not have to build a seat of government when it arrived, because one was standing. Rio had been the capital of the State of Brazil since 1763 and the king’s representative there had been styled Viceroy since then; from 1808 the same city held the government of the whole empire, which some historians call a metropolitan reversal. Forty-four years is a long precondition, and that is what the type says: without it the transfer would have been a different and much harder thing, but 1763 did not bring 1807 about.
